**Surat al-Zalzala (The Earthquake)**
It has eight verses and was revealed in Makkah.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿When the earth is shaken with its (final) earthquake﴾

﴿When the earth is shaken with its (final) earthquake﴾. Here there are several issues.

**The first issue:** The scholars have mentioned several aspects of the connection (munasabah) between the beginning of this surah and the end of the preceding surah.

One of them: when Allah said, ﴿Their reward with their Lord is gardens of perpetual residence﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 8], it is as if the responsible person asked: "And when will that be, O Lord?" So He said, ﴿When the earth is shaken with its (final) earthquake﴾. At that time all the worlds will be in fear, while you, at that time, will receive your reward and will be safe in it, as He said, ﴿And they will be safe from the terror of that Day﴾ [al-Naml: 89].

The second: when Allah mentioned in the preceding surah the threat for the disbelievers and the promise for the believers, He wished to intensify the threat for the disbelievers. So He said: "I will recompense him at the time when the disbeliever mentioned earlier says, ‘What is wrong with the earth, that it is shaken?’" This is similar to His saying: ﴿On the Day when some faces will turn white and some faces will turn black﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106]. Then He mentioned the two groups: ﴿As for those whose faces turn black﴾ [Al 'Imran: 106], and ﴿As for those whose faces turn white﴾ [Al 'Imran: 107]. Then He united them at the end of the surah, mentioning the atom's weight of good and evil.

**The second issue:** Concerning His saying ﴿When﴾ (idha), there are two discussions.

The first: One may say that ﴿idha﴾ denotes a specific time, so how does it fit to begin the surah with it?

Its answer has several aspects:

The first: They used to ask him, "When is the Hour?" So He said, ﴿When the earth is shaken﴾. It is as if He said: "There is no way to specify its time, but I specify it by its signs."

The second: Allah wished to inform the responsible person that the earth will speak and bear witness on the Day of Resurrection, although at this moment it is inanimate. So it was as if it was said: "When will that happen?" And He said, ﴿When the earth is shaken﴾.

The second discussion: They said: The word ﴿in﴾ (in) is used for what is possible, and ﴿idha﴾ is used for what is certain. You say, "If you enter the house, then you are divorced," because entering is possible. But if you intend to attach a condition to something that will certainly occur, you do not say "in," rather you say "idha," as in: "When tomorrow comes, then you are divorced," because it will occur without doubt. This is the original usage. If it contains something contrary to this, it is figurative. Since the earthquake is certain, He said ﴿When [the earth] is shaken﴾.

**The third issue:** Al-Farra' said: "Al-zilzal" with a kasra (zilzal, i.e., al-zilzāl) is the verbal noun (masdar), and "al-zilzal" with a fatha is the noun (ism). Both have been recited. Likewise, "al-waswas" is the name (ism), that is, the name of the devil who whispers to you, while "al-wiswas" with a kasra is the verbal noun. The meaning is: it was moved with a violent movement, as He said: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking﴾ [al-Waqi'ah: 4].

Some people said: The intended meaning of "zulzilat" is not "it was moved," rather the intended meaning is: "it moved and was agitated." The evidence for this is that He speaks of it throughout the surah as He speaks of a being who chooses and has power. Also, this is more effective in inspiring awe, as if He is saying: "Even inanimate matter trembles at the beginnings of the Resurrection. Is it not time for you to tremble and awaken from your heedlessness?" Close to this is His saying: ﴿If you had seen it humbled and split apart out of fear of Allah﴾ [al-Hashr: 21].

Know that "zalla" is for ordinary movement, and "zalzala" is for intense, great movement, because of the meaning of repetition in it. It is like "sarsar" for the wind. Because of the severity of this movement, Allah described it with greatness, saying: ﴿Indeed, the convulsion of the Hour is a tremendous thing﴾ [al-Hajj: 1].

**The fourth issue:** Mujahid said: What is meant by the earthquake mentioned in this verse is the first blast (al-nafkhah al-ula), like His saying: ﴿On the Day the quaking one will quake﴾ ﴿Followed by the following one﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 6–7]. That is, it is shaken at the first blast, then it is shaken a second time, and it brings out its dead, which are the burdens (al-athqal). Others said: This earthquake is the second one, based on the evidence that He made among its consequences that the earth brings out its burdens, and that happens only in the second earthquake.

**The fifth issue:** Concerning His saying ﴿its earthquake﴾ (zilzaluha) with the possessive construction (idafah), there are several aspects:

One: The degree that is fitting for it in wisdom, like your saying: "Honour the righteous with its honour, and humiliate the wicked with its humiliation," meaning the honour and humiliation that they deserve.

The second: The meaning is its whole earthquake and all that is possible from it. The meaning is that every shaking that the place can bear occurred.

The third: ﴿its earthquake﴾ means the one promised for it or written upon it, if it is considered as a living being. Its explanation is what has been narrated: that it is shaken by the intensity of the sound of Israfil, because it is considered as a living being.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 99, verse 2:

As for His saying, ﴿And the earth brings forth its burdens﴾, there are two issues concerning it.

The first issue: Regarding al-athqal (the burdens/loads), there are two opinions.

The first: It is the plural of thaql, which is the goods of the house. [He says:] ﴿And it carries your burdens﴾ [al-Nahl: 7]. He made what is in its belly of treasures burdens for it. Abu 'Ubayda and al-Akhfash said: If the dead person is in the belly of the earth, then he is a burden on it (lahā); if he is above it, then he is a burden upon it (alayhā). It was also said: al-Jinn and al-Insan were called "the two weighty ones" (al-thaqalān) because the earth becomes heavy with them when they are in its belly, and they become heavy upon it when they are on its surface. Then he said: What is meant by this earthquake is the first earthquake. He says: "The earth brings forth its burdens," meaning the treasures, so the surface of the earth becomes filled with gold, and no one pays attention to it. As if the gold were crying out and saying: "Did you not ruin your religion and your worldly life for my sake?" Or the benefit of bringing it out is as He, the Exalted, said: ﴿On the Day when it will be heated in the fire of Hell﴾ [al-Tawba: 35]. And whoever says: What is meant by this earthquake is the second, which is after the Resurrection, he said: It brings forth the burdens, meaning the dead alive, like a mother who gives birth to him alive. It was also said: The earth expels him dead as he was buried, then Allah, the Exalted, brings him to life.

The second opinion:

Its burdens: its secrets. So on that Day the secrets will be revealed, and for this reason He said: ﴿On that Day it will relate its news﴾, so that it bears witness for you or against you.

The second issue: He, the Exalted, said describing the earth: ﴿Have We not made the earth a receptacle?﴾ [al-Mursalat: 25]. Then it became in a state that throws you out, and this is a confirmation of His saying: ﴿Every nursing mother will be distracted from what she nursed﴾ [al-Hajj: 2], and His saying: ﴿On the Day a man will flee﴾ [Abasa: 34].

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 99, verses 3–4:

As for His saying, exalted is He, ﴿And man will say, "What is wrong with it?"﴾ ﴿That Day it will report its news﴾, there are several issues:

The first issue: "What is wrong with it, that it is shaken with this violent shaking and has cast out what is in its belly?" This happens either at the first blast (nafkha, the blast of the Trumpet), when it casts out what is within it of treasures and hoards, or at the second blast, when it casts out what is within it of the dead.

The second issue: It is said that this is the saying of the disbelievers, who say, as they say: ﴿Who has raised us up from our sleeping place?﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52]. As for the believer, he says: ﴿This is what the Most Merciful promised, and the messengers spoke truly﴾ [Ya-Sin: 52]. It is also said: rather, it is general concerning both the believer and the disbeliever, meaning: the human being, who is ungrateful (kanud), anxious (jaz'u), and wrongdoing (zalum), whose nature is heedlessness and ignorance, says, "What is wrong with it?" and this is not a question but an expression of wonder at the marvels he sees, which no ear has heard of and no tongue has described. For this reason al-Hasan said: it is for the disbeliever and the wicked alike.

The third issue: He said, ﴿What is wrong with it?﴾ in the third person rather than the second person, because he is rebuking his own self through this speech, as if he were saying: "O self, what is wrong with the earth that it does this?" meaning: O self, you are the cause of it, for were it not for your disobediences the earth would not have become like this. So the disbelievers say this statement, while the believers say: ﴿And they will say, "Praise be to God, who has removed from us the grief"﴾ [Fatir: 34].

As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That Day it will report its news﴾, know that Ibn Mas'ud recited: "Tunbi'u akhbarahā" (it will inform of its news), and Sa'id ibn Jubayr recited "Tunabbi'u" (it will be made to inform). Then there are questions:

The first: Where are the two objects of tuhaddithu (it will report)?

The answer: The first of them has been omitted, and the second is "akhbārahā" (its news). The original would be "tuhaddithu al-khalqa akhbārahā" (it reports to the creation its news), but the intended point is the mention of its reporting the news, not the mention of the creation, as an exaltation.

The second question: What is the meaning of the earth's reporting? We say: there are several aspects:

One of them, which is the saying of Abu Muslim: "That Day it will become clear to everyone the recompense of his deed," so it is as if it had reported this, just as you say: "The house tells us that it was inhabited." Likewise, the disintegration of the earth through the shaking reports that the world has ended and the Hereafter has come.

The second, which is the saying of the majority: God, exalted is He, makes the earth a living, rational, speaking creature, and informs it of everything the people of it did; then on that Day it bears witness for whoever obeyed and against whoever disobeyed. He, peace be upon him, said: "Indeed the earth will inform on the Day of Resurrection of every deed done upon it," and then he recited this verse. This, according to our school, is not far-fetched, because physical structure is not, in our view, a condition for accepting life. The earth, while remaining in its form, dryness and roughness, God creates in it life and speech. The point is as if the earth complains against the disobedient and thanks whoever obeyed God, saying: "So-and-so prayed, paid zakat, fasted and performed the Hajj upon me, and so-and-so disbelieved, committed adultery, stole and oppressed," until the disbeliever wishes that he be driven to the Fire. ʿAli, peace be upon him, when the treasury (bayt al-mal) was emptied, would pray two rak'ahs in it and say: "Let it bear witness that I filled you with truth and emptied you with truth."

The third view, which is the view of the Mu'tazila: speech may be created in inanimate matter, so it is not far-fetched that God, exalted is He, may create in the earth, while it is inanimate, distinct articulated sounds; thus the speaker and the witness under this supposition would be God, exalted is He.

The third question: What governs "idhā" (when) and "yawma'idhin" (that Day)? The answer: "yawma'idhin" is a substitute (badal) for "idhā," and its governing word is "tuhaddithu."

The fourth question: The word "tahdith" (reporting) implies intimacy and comfort, whereas there is no intimacy there, so what is the reason for this word? The answer: the earth is, as it were, pouring out its complaint to the friends of God and His angels.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 99, verses 5–6:

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Because your Lord has inspired it﴾ ﴿On that Day, people will come forth in scattered groups to be shown their deeds﴾, there are two questions.

The first question: With what is the bā' in His saying ﴿Because (bi-anna) your Lord﴾ connected? The answer: It is connected to "tuhaddithu" (it will relate), and its meaning is: it will relate its news because your Lord has inspired it.

The second question: Why did He not say awḥā ilayhā (inspired to it)? The answer: There are two aspects to this.

The first: Abu 'Ubayda said: ﴿awḥā lahā﴾ means awḥā ilayhā (inspired to it), and he recited the verse of al-'Ajjaj:

"He inspired to it (lahā) the settled ground, so it settled."

The second: Perhaps He only said lahā (for it), meaning: We did that for its sake, so that the earth may attain satisfaction by means of that from the disobedient.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿On that Day, people will come forth in scattered groups to be shown their deeds﴾. Ṣudūr is the opposite of wurūd. So the wārid (one who arrives) is the one who comes, and the ṣādir (one who departs) is the one who turns away. Ashtātan means scattered, dispersed. It is possible that they arrive at the earth and then depart from the earth to the plain of the Resurrection. It is also possible that they arrive at the plain of the Resurrection for reckoning and then depart from it to the place of reward and punishment. The word ashtātan is closer to the first aspect, and the word ṣadr is closer to the second aspect. His saying ﴿to be shown their deeds﴾ is closer to the first aspect, because seeing their deeds written in the records is closer to the literal reality than seeing the recompense of deeds, although it is also valid to interpret it as seeing the recompense of deeds. His saying ﴿ashtātan﴾ has several aspects:

First: some of them go to the place of standing mounted, with fine garments and bright faces, while the herald proclaims before them: "This is a friend of God." Others are led with black faces, barefoot and naked, with chains and shackles, while the herald proclaims before them: "This is an enemy of God."

Second: ashtātan means each group with its own kind: the Jew with the Jew, and the Christian with the Christian.

Third: ashtātan means from the regions of the earth, from every direction. Then He, glorified is He, mentioned the purpose and said: ﴿to be shown their deeds﴾. Some said: to be shown the records of their deeds, because writing is placed before a man and he says: "This is your divorce and your sale," and does he see it? The thing seen is the writing. Others said: to be shown the recompense of their deeds, which is Paradise or Hell. The name of "deed" was applied to the recompense only because it is a recompense corresponding to it, so it is as if it were the deed itself; indeed the metaphor in this is more fitting than the literal sense. In the recitation of the Prophet (ﷺ) it is "li-yaraw" with a fatḥa.

Commentary of al-Razi (Mafatih al-Ghayb) on surah 99, verses 7–8:

Then the Exalted said: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾ ﴿and whoever does an atom's weight of evil will see it﴾. And in this there are several issues:

The first issue: ﴿mithqala dharra﴾ means the weight of an atom (dharra). Al-Kalbi said: the dharra is the smallest ant. Ibn 'Abbas said: if you place your palm on the earth and then lift it, each particle of dust that clings to it is a mithqal dharra. There is no servant who does good or evil, little or much, except that Allah the Exalted shows it to him.

The second issue: In a narration from 'Asim, the reading is "yurahu" with a damma on the ya'. The rest of the readers read ﴿yarahu﴾ with a fatha on it, and some read "yarah" with a jazm (sukun).

The third issue: There is a difficulty in the verse, namely that the good deeds of the disbeliever are nullified by his disbelief, and the bad deeds of the believer are forgiven, either from the outset or because of avoiding the major sins. So what is the meaning of being recompensed with atoms' weights of good and evil?

Know that the exegetes answered this in several ways:

The first: Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: ﴿whoever does an atom's weight﴾ of good while being a disbeliever, he sees the reward for that in this world until he meets the Hereafter, and he has nothing in it. This is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas. What confirms the soundness of this interpretation is what is reported that he (ﷺ) said to Abu Bakr: "O Abu Bakr, whatever you see in this world of what you dislike is an atom's weight of evil, and Allah stores up for you atoms' weights of good until you are paid them in full on the Day of Resurrection."

The second: Ibn 'Abbas said: no believer or disbeliever does good or evil except that Allah shows it to him. As for the believer, Allah forgives his evil deeds and rewards him for his good deeds; as for the disbeliever, his good deeds are rejected and he is punished for his evil deeds.

The third: The good deeds of the disbeliever, although nullified by his disbelief, the weighing is still taken into account, so those good deeds are assessed as having been cancelled out by the punishment for his disbelief. The same is said of the other side, and so this does not undermine the generality of the verse.

The fourth: We specify the generality of His saying: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾, and we say: the meaning is, whoever among the fortunate does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever among the wretched does an atom's weight of evil will see it.

The fourth issue: Someone may say: if the matter is to this extent, where is the generosity? The answer: this is the generosity, because disobedience, however little, carries disrespect, and the Generous does not tolerate it; and in obedience there is honour, and however little it is, the Generous does not waste it. It is as if the Exalted were saying: do not consider an atom's weight of good to be small, for you, despite your baseness and weakness, did not waste My atom; rather you took it into account, reflected upon it, drew evidence from it for My essence and attributes, and made it a vehicle by which you reached Me. So if you did not waste My atom, shall I waste your atom! Then the verification is that the intention and purpose are what matter: if the deed is small but the intention is sincere, the goal has been attained; and if the deed is great but the intention is divided, the purpose is lost. Among this is what is reported from Ka'b: "Do not belittle anything of kindness, for a man entered Paradise because of lending a needle in the way of Allah, and a woman helped with a grain in building Bayt al-Maqdis and entered Paradise." And from 'Aisha: "Grapes were before her, and she offered them to the women present in her presence. A beggar came, and she ordered that he be given a single grape from them. Some of those who were with her laughed, and she said: 'Indeed, in what you see is an atom's weight,' and she recited this verse." Perhaps her purpose was teaching, otherwise she was at the utmost of generosity. It is reported: "Ibn al-Zubayr sent her one hundred and eighty thousand dirhams in two sacks, and she called for a tray and began distributing it among the people. When evening came she said: 'O servant girl, bring my iftar, come here.' So she brought bread and oil. It was said to her: 'Did you not keep back one dirham for us to buy meat with which to break our fast?' She said: 'If you had reminded me, I would have done so.'"

Muqatil said: this verse was revealed concerning two men. One of them, when a beggar came to him, considered it too little to give him a date, a morsel or a nut, and would say, "This is nothing; we are rewarded only for what we give." The other would be careless about a minor sin, saying, "There is nothing upon me for this; the threat of the Fire is only for the major sins." So this verse was revealed as an encouragement toward a little good, for it is near that it will increase, and a warning against a small sin, for it is near that it will grow. For this reason he (ﷺ) said: "Guard yourselves against the Fire even with half a date; and whoever does not find it, then with a good word." And Allah the Exalted knows best, and may Allah send blessings upon our master Muhammad, and upon his family and companions, and grant them peace.

Ibn 'Abbas said: if you place your palm on the earth and then lift it, each particle of dust that clings to it is a mithqal dharra. There is no servant who does good or evil, little or much, except that Allah the Exalted shows it to him.

The second issue: In a narration from 'Asim, the reading is "yurahu" with a damma on the ya'. The rest of the readers read ﴿yarahu﴾ with a fatha on it, and some read "yarah" with a jazm (sukun).

The third issue: There is a difficulty in the verse, namely that the good deeds of the disbeliever are nullified by his disbelief, and the bad deeds of the believer are forgiven, either from the outset or because of avoiding the major sins. So what is the meaning of being recompensed with atoms' weights of good and evil?

Know that the exegetes answered this in several ways:

The first: Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: ﴿whoever does an atom's weight﴾ of good while being a disbeliever, he sees the reward for that in this world until he meets the Hereafter, and he has nothing in it. This is also reported from Ibn 'Abbas. What confirms the soundness of this interpretation is what is reported that he (ﷺ) said to Abu Bakr: "O Abu Bakr, whatever you see in this world of what you dislike is an atom's weight of evil, and Allah stores up for you atoms' weights of good until you are paid them in full on the Day of Resurrection."

The second: Ibn 'Abbas said: no believer or disbeliever does good or evil except that Allah shows it to him. As for the believer, Allah forgives his evil deeds and rewards him for his good deeds; as for the disbeliever, his good deeds are rejected and he is punished for his evil deeds.

The third: The good deeds of the disbeliever, although nullified by his disbelief, the weighing is still taken into account, so those good deeds are assessed as having been cancelled out by the punishment for his disbelief. The same is said of the other side, and so this does not undermine the generality of the verse.

The fourth: We specify the generality of His saying: ﴿So whoever does an atom's weight of good will see it﴾, and we say: the meaning is, whoever among the fortunate does an atom's weight of good will see it, and whoever among the wretched does an atom's weight of evil will see it.

The fourth issue: Someone may say: if the matter is to this extent, where is the generosity? The answer: this is the generosity, because disobedience, however little, carries disrespect, and the Generous does not tolerate it; and in obedience there is honour, and however little it is, the Generous does not waste it. It is as if the Exalted were saying: do not consider an atom's weight of good to be small, for you, despite your baseness and weakness, did not waste My atom; rather you took it into account, reflected upon it, drew evidence from it for My essence and attributes, and made it a vehicle by which you reached Me. So if you did not waste My atom, shall I waste your atom! Then the verification is that the intention and purpose are what matter: if the deed is small but the intention is sincere, the goal has been attained; and if the deed is great but the intention is divided, the purpose is lost. Among this is what is reported from Ka'b: "Do not belittle anything of kindness, for a man entered Paradise because of lending a needle in the way of Allah, and a woman helped with a grain in building Bayt al-Maqdis and entered Paradise." And from 'Aisha: "Grapes were before her, and she offered them to the women present in her presence. A beggar came, and she ordered that he be given a single grape from them. Some of those who were with her laughed, and she said: 'Indeed, in what you see is an atom's weight,' and she recited this verse." Perhaps her purpose was teaching, otherwise she was at the utmost of generosity. It is reported: "Ibn al-Zubayr sent her one hundred and eighty thousand dirhams in two sacks, and she called for a tray and began distributing it among the people. When evening came she said: 'O servant girl, bring my iftar, come here.' So she brought bread and oil. It was said to her: 'Did you not keep back one dirham for us to buy meat with which to break our fast?' She said: 'If you had reminded me, I would have done so.'"

Page 59

Muqatil said: this verse was revealed concerning two men. One of them, when a beggar came to him, considered it too little to give him a date, a morsel or a nut, and would say, "This is nothing; we are rewarded only for what we give." The other would be careless about a minor sin, saying, "There is nothing upon me for this; the threat of the Fire is only for the major sins." So this verse was revealed as an encouragement toward a little good, for it is near that it will increase, and a warning against a small sin, for it is near that it will grow. For this reason he (ﷺ) said: "Guard yourselves against the Fire even with half a date; and whoever does not find it, then with a good word." And Allah the Exalted knows best, and may Allah send blessings upon our master Muhammad, and upon his family and companions, and grant them peace.
